clue.text: Spout brilliance on trip, in telling good stories for company?

indicators.note: a person on a trip is reeling and lurching about, so the letters of the two preceding words are tumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to gush with wit while travelling, spinning yarns to keep their companions amused.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'company' as a business, not fellow travellers: PR people tell flattering stories about a firm. The fifteen letters of SPOUT and BRILLIANCE, shaken up by 'on trip', give the answer exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporate publicity is the craft of putting out favourable accounts of a firm, so it means telling good stories on a business's behalf.

clue.text: What was enlivened by 29, or another account of spiritual journey

explanation.surface: The Canterbury pilgrims' road was livened up by their yarns, and there is a second famous book about a soul's journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: the progress of Chaucer's pilgrims to Canterbury was livened up by the travellers' tales at 29. The second is Bunyan's allegory of the same name, a different account of a spiritual journey.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's band of travellers made their way to the shrine telling stories, and Bunyan's 1678 Christian allegory carries this title too.

clue.text: Queen's in cabin in stern of yacht at sea? Her Majesty is

indicators.note: being at sea means being confused or all over the place, so the gathered letters are mixed up

parts.note: R, for Regina, is the standard abbreviation for a queen

indicators.note: the stern is the back end of a boat, so the clue wants the final letter of the word yacht

explanation.surface: A monarch sits in a cabin at the back of a yacht on the ocean, and the royal title is mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: R, IN, CABIN and T (the last letter of yacht) are rearranged. The definition completes the old royal style 'Her Britannic Majesty', the formal title of the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The monarch of the United Kingdom was formally styled with this adjective, meaning of Britain, before the word Majesty.

clue.text: As citizen of republic, is one imprisoning king after rising?

indicators.note: imprisoning means holding something inside, so the king's name goes within the pair formed by is and one

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so the king's name is turned backwards

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's legendary king of Britain

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether, as a member of a republic, one would lock up a monarch after an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after rising' reverses LEAR to RAEL, which goes inside IS + I. 'rising' looks like a revolt against the king, but in a down clue it means the letters go upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel is a parliamentary republic, and a national of that state carries this demonym.

clue.text: Changes from spiritual instruction, seldom converted

parts.note: RE stands for religious education, a school subject in Britain

indicators.note: converted means changed into a different form, so the letters of seldom are rearranged

explanation.surface: A religious teacher's lessons rarely turn anyone to the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is followed by MODELS, the anagram of SELDOM made by 'converted'. 'converted' plays on religious conversion to suit the spiritual surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To remould or rework something is to alter it, so the verb in the third person matches 'changes'.

clue.text: Group of acids I kept under pressure inside covers

indicators.note: inside means the pair of letters is placed within the word for covers

parts.note: lids are covers for pots or boxes

indicators.note: in a down clue, being kept under means sitting below, so the letter I comes after the letter for pressure

parts.note: P is the standard symbol for pressure in physics

explanation.surface: A person tells of being held down under strain beneath the bedclothes.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'kept under' puts I below P, giving PI, which goes inside LIDS after its first two letters. 'covers' suggests bedclothes but means lids.
explanation.definitionFit: Fats, oils and waxes form a class of fatty-acid compounds in biochemistry, which this plural names.

clue.text: Inclined to save most of the split money, ultimately

indicators.note: most of a word means it is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a rift is a split or break

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word money

explanation.surface: A careful person keeps most of the divided cash, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: TH (the without its last letter) + RIFT + Y (the end of money).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone frugal tends to put money by rather than spend it.

clue.text: Indications of doubt in credo believer harboured

indicators.note: harboured means sheltered within, so the answer sits inside the run of letters credo believer

explanation.surface: A believer's creed holds signs of uncertainty.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is in credO BELIever. These marks were used by ancient scribes to flag doubtful passages in manuscripts.
explanation.definitionFit: Editors of old texts used a dagger or a short dash, called an obelus, to mark a spurious or questionable passage; this is its plural.

clue.text: Second collection of leaves for gentleman in the country

parts.note: a quire is a set of sheets of paper, traditionally twenty-four or twenty-five

explanation.surface: A further bundle of pages is set aside for a country gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' suggests foliage on a rural estate, but here they are sheets of paper. A squire is the chief landowner in an English village.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal landowner of an English rural parish was traditionally called by this title.

clue.text: Garland of flowers cut in part of Ireland

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian flower garland
to trim is to cut

explanation.surface: A floral wreath is cut back somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Leitrim is a county in the north-west of the Republic of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a county in the province of Connacht, a region of the Irish Republic.

clue.text: Crashed rave-up introducing new, emergent celebrity

indicators.note: introducing means bringing something in, so the letter for new is placed inside the rearranged party
crashed means wrecked or smashed up, so the letters of rave-up are broken into a new order

explanation.surface: A newcomer gatecrashes a wild party, a rising star on the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crashed' turns RAVEUP into PARVEU, and 'introducing' slips N in before the U. A rave-up is a lively party, and the surface suggests gatecrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstart who has risen suddenly to wealth or fame, without the background to match, is a social climber of this kind.

clue.text: With a lot of paper completed, did another round of editing

parts.note: a ream is a large quantity of paper, 500 sheets
ended means completed

explanation.surface: An editor finishes a big stack of pages and goes over the text again.
explanation.walkthrough: REAM + ENDED, joined by 'With'.
explanation.definitionFit: To revise a text a second time is to alter it once more, a further correction.

clue.text: Man with order coming back from our Air Force

indicators.note: coming back says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A man under orders returns from serving in the national air force.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters hide in ouR AIR Force and are read backwards. 'order' suggests military orders, but it is a religious order such as the Franciscans.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a mendicant religious brotherhood, such as a Dominican or Franciscan, belongs to an order.

clue.text: Purchaser of provisions — in principle, fellow replacing almost half

indicators.note: the word fellow is swapped in for nearly half of the letters of principle, its first four of nine

parts.note: a man is a fellow

explanation.surface: A buyer of supplies has, in theory, someone standing in for most of half the job.
explanation.walkthrough: PRINCIPLE has nine letters; its first four, PRIN, are almost half, and MAN replaces them. A manciple bought food for a college or inn of court, and one is a Canterbury pilgrim.
explanation.definitionFit: A steward who bought food and stores for a college, monastery or inn of court held this office.

clue.text: Person turning yellow, initially, into another colour?

indicators.note: into means the letter is placed inside the reversed colour
turning means the colour's word is spun round to read backwards

parts.note: red is another colour besides yellow

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word yellow

explanation.surface: Someone changes yellow cloth to a different shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses RED to DER, and the first letter of yellow goes 'into' it. The whole clue also describes what this tradesperson does, so the surface doubles as a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesperson who colours cloth or yarn changes its shade for a living.

clue.text: Go in with lure, haphazardly trapping unknown bird

indicators.note: trapping means catching inside, so the unknown letter goes within the jumbled letters
haphazardly means at random, so the letters of go in and lure are jumbled

parts.note: Z is a standard algebraic unknown, like x and y

explanation.surface: A hunter goes in with bait, carelessly snaring a mysterious bird.
explanation.walkthrough: GO IN and LURE are jumbled by 'haphazardly', with Z placed inside by 'trapping'. The ring ouzel is a thrush of upland Britain with a white band on its chest.
explanation.definitionFit: This upland thrush, black with a white crescent across its breast, is a species of songbird.

clue.text: Becomes admirer of pro after some seasons in US

indicators.note: after places the word for pro behind the seasons

parts.note: Americans call autumn the fall, so several autumns are falls
for means in favour of, as pro does

explanation.surface: Someone takes a liking to a professional after a few American autumns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pro' looks like a professional, but it is the Latin 'for', in favour of.
explanation.definitionFit: To be smitten with someone is to become attracted to them, a phrasal verb for starting to love.

clue.text: See 1 Down
Famous captain who's in charge of steamer?

explanation.surface: A celebrated sea captain is asked who runs the steamship.
explanation.walkthrough: The first is Captain James Cook, the explorer. 'steamer' is a pan for steaming food, not a ship, so the second is whoever prepares the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: James Cook charted the Pacific in the eighteenth century; in a kitchen, the person handling a steaming pan prepares the food.

clue.text: Old girl we intimidate

parts.note: Vera is a girl's name

explanation.surface: An old woman and the rest of us frighten people.
explanation.walkthrough: O + VERA + WE.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill someone with awe so that they are cowed is to subdue them by fear or respect.

clue.text: He lets people off between two and six? It's a bargain, right

parts.note: par for a golf hole is three, four or five strokes, so it falls between two and six
done! is said to agree a deal

explanation.surface: Someone offers clemency in mid-week, shaking hands on a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: PAR + DONE + R. A pardoner sold indulgences in medieval times, and Chaucer's Pardoner is one of the Canterbury pilgrims.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval seller of papal indulgences offered sinners forgiveness, so he releases people from punishment.

clue.text: Get to talk with random selection of players in public

parts.note: a draw pairs players or teams by lot, as in a cup draw
out means openly known, in public view

explanation.surface: Someone coaxes a conversation while the line-up of players is chosen at random in full view.
explanation.walkthrough: DRAW + OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To coax a shy person into conversation is to get them to open up.

clue.text: Bother about river one found for fishing club

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for bother goes round the letters for river and one

parts.note: a pest is a nuisance or bother
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: An angler grumbles about a river where they found a fishing society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' suggests a society of anglers, but it is a short cudgel used to kill a caught fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A small weighted cudgel for killing landed fish is called by this name, from its giving them last rites.

clue.text: Sailors are prone to climb and descend

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, ordinary sailors

indicators.note: in a down clue, to climb means to read upwards, so the word is turned backwards

parts.note: to lie is to be prone, flat on the ground

explanation.surface: Seamen tend to go up the rigging and come down by rope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climb' reverses LIE to EIL in this down clue. The surface contrasts climbing and descending, but 'climb' only turns the word around.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower oneself down a rock face on a doubled rope is to come down by roping.

clue.text: Pass through centre of Berkshire, eventually

indicators.note: the answer lies in the middle of the words that follow, straddling the gap between them

explanation.surface: Someone drives across the middle of an English county in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters hide in berkshiRE EVEntually. To reeve is a nautical verb: to pass a rope through a ring or block. A reeve is also a Canterbury pilgrim.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors thread a rope through a pulley or eye with this verb, so it means to pass it through.

clue.text: Plant exhibited by Central Americans

indicators.note: central picks the letters at the centre of the following word, dropping its outer pairs

explanation.surface: A shrub is on show among the people of Central America.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle five letters of AMERICANS. 'Central Americans' reads as people from Central America, but 'Central' is a selection signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Heather belongs to a genus of low evergreen shrubs whose botanical name is this.

clue.text: Put extra back in large pool

indicators.note: in places the reversed extra inside the word for large

parts.note: big means large

indicators.note: back means the word for the extra is read in reverse

parts.note: a no ball is an extra in cricket, a run awarded for an illegal delivery

explanation.surface: Someone tells you to put an additional amount back into a big swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses NO BALL to LLABON, which goes inside BIG. A billabong is an Australian pool left in a cut-off river bend.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia, a stagnant backwater or oxbow lake left behind by a river is known by this name.

clue.text: I run into European friend in part of the Middle East

indicators.note: into places I and the letter for run inside the European friend

parts.note: mate means friend
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Someone bumps into a European pal in the Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: E + MATE, with I + R placed 'into' it after the M.
explanation.definitionFit: A state ruled by an emir, such as Qatar or Kuwait, is a territory of this kind.

clue.text: Return of mayhem in disturbed life of disreputable girl

indicators.note: in places the reversed word for mayhem inside the rearranged life
disturbed means stirred up, so the letters of life are rearranged
return means the word for mayhem comes back the other way, read backwards

parts.note: a zoo is a scene of chaos or mayhem

explanation.surface: A loose woman's troubled existence sees chaos come back again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return of' turns ZOO into OOZ, which goes inside FLIE, the anagram of LIFE made by 'disturbed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman thought loose or promiscuous is slangily called this, a dated word for a tart.

clue.text: Tall stories from 8, 12, et al.

explanation.surface: Exaggerated yarns are told by a squire, a friar and others.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is exaggerated, unlikely stories. The second is literal: the Squire, the Friar and the other Canterbury pilgrims are travellers who each tell a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarns from journeys are proverbially exaggerated, and Chaucer's pilgrims on the road to Canterbury each tell a story.
